The study focused on minimizing **junction area variation/fluctuation**, identified in the local source as the dominant driver of Josephson-junction critical-current non-uniformity [arxiv-2210.15293].

Reported related figures: resistance variation of **9.8–4.4%** across **22 × 22 mm²** chips and **4.8–2.3%** across **5 × 10 mm²** chips; linewidth standard deviation **4 nm** over **4500 junctions** with areas **0.008–0.12 μm²** [arxiv-2210.15293].

The local KB says the design choice is a **shared SQUID integrated into the two transmon qubits**, intended to provide strong parametric coupling while **avoiding internal coupler excitations** and minimizing added control/readout ports [arxiv-2305.02907].

They emphasize non-RWA terms because their measured qubit–resonator detunings are small enough that standard RWA extraction is not valid: the 6-xmon devices have detunings of only about `Δ/2π ≈ 0.5–1.7 GHz`, comparable to typical transmon anharmonicity, so counter-rotating terms materially affect the inferred dispersive shift/coupling. Using the non-RWA treatment lets the simulation-experiment comparison report a qubit–resonator coupling-rate RMS error of `10.4%`; the same source also reports RMS errors of `4.1%` for anharmonicity, `16.9%` for resonator linewidth, and `3.8%` for resonator frequency. [arxiv-2312.13483]

The AWS CQC experiment used a noise-biased transmon-to-cat CX gate with an approximately chi-matched dispersive interaction, engineered so first-order ancilla relaxation from `|f⟩` to `|e⟩` during the gate did not strongly induce target cat-qubit bit flips, thereby preserving the cat-qubit noise bias during syndrome extraction [arxiv-2409.13025].

The local source summary gives no more specific implementation detail or exact numerical suppression factor for this mechanism.

The Tanner graph is suitable because its connectivity can be realized as the edge graph of a modular superconducting layout: long-range couplers between chip modules implement the nonlocal LDPC Tanner-graph edges even though the graph is not locally embeddable in a 2D grid. The local KB links this to multi-chip tunable-coupler hardware, but it does not provide exact coupling-length numbers for the Bravyi et al. paper in the retrieved summary evidence. [arxiv-2308.07915]

Flag qubits are essential because the heavy square decoder relies on their nontrivial outcomes to reweight the minimum-weight-perfect-matching graph and thereby account for correlated data errors caused by weight-four syndrome-measurement fault propagation. The local KB says this flag-informed reweighting is what “restores correction up to the full code distance,” so flags are part of the decoding information, not merely optional syndrome-extraction ancillas [arxiv-1907.09528].

The evidence also says that ignoring flag information substantially worsens heavy square performance: the heavy-square logical X/Z thresholds are approximately `0.3%` with the flag-qubit decoding protocol, while ignoring flags gives an X-error threshold near `0.2%` and logical Z rates about an order of magnitude worse [arxiv-1907.09528].

The floating metal “bones” in the Skeleton 3D transmon were intended to alter the balance of surface participation, specifically changing substrate-vacuum versus substrate-metal participation so the design could help probe surface-loss mechanisms [arxiv-1509.03859].

Transmon transition frequencies are usually chosen around `4–8 GHz` because this range balances several device constraints: it is high enough that the qubit thermal excitation is well suppressed in a dilution refrigerator, but low enough to stay below the superconducting gap frequency and avoid quasiparticle-generation losses; it also lies in a practical microwave-control/readout band for cQED devices [aps-10.1103-PRXQuantum.2.040202].

Google chose adjustable couplers because a fixed-coupling architecture left too much unwanted two-qubit interaction idle: fixed coupling would make residual interactions “always on,” limiting simultaneous operation and increasing crosstalk/errors. The Sycamore tunable-transmon architecture instead used tunable couplers to turn interactions on for entangling gates and suppress them otherwise, enabling a dense 2D nearest-neighbor processor with parallel gates [arxiv-1910.11333].

The local KB summary also grounds the associated Sycamore metrics: 53 working qubits, single-qubit gate error \(0.16\% \pm 0.03\%\), two-qubit gate error \(0.62\% \pm 0.16\%\), and simultaneous two-qubit gate error \(0.93\% \pm 0.21\%\) [nature-s41586-019-1666-5].

scqubits handles these coloring artifacts by providing an interactive remedy: the user can click on misassigned branch segments in a transition plot to manually adjust the coloring when avoided crossings invalidate the dispersive-limit product-state labels [arxiv-2107.08552].

Heavy-square and heavy-hexagon lattices could use a three-frequency pattern because their lower connectivity allows neighboring qubits to be assigned one of three target frequencies while still keeping every connected pair outside the paper’s defined cross-resonance collision windows [arxiv-2009.00781].

The source gives the three-frequency placement as `5.0 GHz`, `5.1 GHz`, and `5.2 GHz`; with LASIQ trimming, the optimized post-anneal frequency spread was reported as `18.5 MHz` for heavy-square and `18.1 MHz` for heavy-hexagon [arxiv-2009.00781].

The collision-avoidance condition in the KB summary is that CR processor yield is limited by frequency crowding/collisions, and the LASIQ-tuned layouts were evaluated against the listed CR collision constraints; the heavy-square/heavy-hexagon three-frequency layouts met those constraints in the reported simulations, unlike more constrained frequency allocations [arxiv-2009.00781].

The proposal uses **opposite-sign anharmonicities**: the tunable C-shunt flux coupler is designed with **positive anharmonicity**, while the transmon qubits have their usual **negative anharmonicity**. This sign inversion is the mechanism used to make the zero-ZZ condition compatible with maximal computational-basis localization [arxiv-2306.17007].

The current `knowledge-base/` does not contain the needed rationale for the `d−1` bridge choice.

The only matching local source is a summary of “Tour de gross,” but it does not include the specific explanation for why the adapter stops at bridge size `d−1` rather than adding one more bridge qubit to reach full deformed code distance `d` for inter-module measurements [arxiv-2506.03094].

The mechanism is interference from the braided multi-point coupling geometry: relaxation into the waveguide is cancelled at the decoherence-free frequency by destructive interference between emission paths, but the waveguide-mediated exchange remains finite because the braided ordering makes the coherent exchange interference condition different from the decay-cancellation condition. Thus the device suppresses spontaneous emission without turning off coherent qubit–qubit coupling [nature-s41586-020-2529-9].

The local KB source does not give the exact exchange value or uncertainty for the two-point braided device; it only states that the exchange is finite at the decoherence-free frequency [nature-s41586-020-2529-9].

The transmon differs from a conventional Cooper pair box by operating the same CPB circuit in a much larger Josephson-to-charging-energy regime, increasing \(E_J/E_C\) to about \(50\) instead of the CPB-like \(E_J/E_C \sim 1\) regime [aps-10.1103-PhysRevA.76.042319].

This suppresses charge-noise sensitivity because the charge dispersion of the low-lying transition frequencies decreases exponentially with \(\sqrt{E_J/E_C}\), making the qubit frequency nearly insensitive to offset charge fluctuations [aps-10.1103-PhysRevA.76.042319]. It does not eliminate controllability because the levels remain weakly anharmonic: at \(E_J/E_C = 50\), the source reports an anharmonicity of roughly \(200\)–\(300\) MHz, still sufficient for selective microwave control of the qubit transition [aps-10.1103-PhysRevA.76.042319].

A plain LC oscillator has a harmonic, equally spaced spectrum, so driving the `|0⟩→|1⟩` transition would also excite higher transitions. Inserting a Josephson junction supplies the required nonlinearity: its nonlinear inductance makes the circuit spectrum anharmonic, so the lowest two levels can be spectrally isolated and used as a qubit subspace rather than as one mode of a harmonic oscillator [aip-10.1063-1.5089550].

The local KB summary gives this mechanism qualitatively but does not provide exact numerical anharmonicities, units, or uncertainties for this point [aip-10.1063-1.5089550].

Replacing the transmon’s single Josephson junction with an asymmetric SQUID loop gives the qubit **in-situ frequency tunability**, so each qubit’s transition frequency can be adjusted after fabrication by applying magnetic flux through the loop [aip-10.1063-1.5089550].

That helps practical quantum-processor design because post-fabrication tuning lets engineers compensate fabrication scatter, place qubits at desired operating frequencies, and avoid unwanted spectral collisions in multi-qubit chips [aip-10.1063-1.5089550]. The asymmetry keeps the flux-tunable transmon from tuning all the way to zero effective Josephson energy, giving a finite tunability range rather than complete suppression of the qubit frequency [aip-10.1063-1.5089550].

The credited design choice was using an **inductively coupled fluxonium design** that behaves nearly like **transversely coupled spin-1/2 systems**, enabling selective-darkening control while suppressing quantum crosstalk without extra couplers or non-computational transitions. The reported result was a **60 ns direct `CX_pi` gate**, **99.94%** fidelity, remaining **above 99.9% for 24 days without recalibration** [arxiv-2407.15783].

The small junction is shunted by a series array of larger-area tunnel junctions because the array provides a large kinetic inductance while avoiding the problems of an ordinary wire: ordinary-wire parasitics would destroy the desired charging regime needed for strong flux fluctuations. The larger-junction array also suppresses unwanted phase slips/parasitic resonances under design conditions and screens quasistatic offset charges because all superconducting islands are connected through at least one large junction. The implemented circuit used 43 Al-AlOx-Al array junctions plus the small junction; a 72-hour spectroscopy data set showed no observable jumps or drifts, supporting offset-charge immunity in that device. [arxiv-0906.0831]

Apertures were patterned in the carrier chip’s niobium metallization directly opposite the qubits to remove metal near the qubits and thereby reduce dielectric losses from the lossy metal/air interface [arxiv-2505.04337].

A simple ideal transmission line is not a suitable subsystem candidate because the modular quasi-lumped method requires each subsystem to be a compact unit whose electromagnetic behavior can be represented by a small lumped/quasi-lumped network. An ideal transmission line instead has distributed modes along its length, so treating it as a standalone subsystem would not yield the compact finite set of lumped parameters needed for the method’s Hamiltonian extraction workflow [arxiv-2103.10344].

The differential AC-Stark-shift (SiZZle/CZ-style) architecture improves fabrication yield because its entangling-drive frequency is tunable, adding a degree of freedom that helps avoid frequency-collision constraints after fabrication variation. In contrast, cross-resonance yield is limited by stricter fixed-frequency collision constraints among qubits, gate drives, and spectator transitions; qutrit CR adds still more constraints and further reduces yield [arxiv-2112.01634].

The local KB source states the comparison qualitatively: for an 8-qubit ring, CR-qubit yield is low at state-of-the-art dispersion, while the differential AC-Stark-shift architecture reaches much higher yield because the entangling-drive frequency can vary; for larger tiled lattices, CR-based 1,000-qubit collision-free lattices are unlikely under demonstrated fabrication dispersion, whereas AC-Stark-shift can reach 1,000-qubit scale for some lattices with postprocessing-level dispersion [arxiv-2112.01634].

No exact numerical yields, units, or uncertainties are present in the available local source summary.

The processor used a **tunable coupler architecture**: two fluxonium qubits were coupled through an intermediate coupler whose flux bias could tune the effective interaction, suppressing unwanted static qubit-qubit crosstalk while enabling activated two-qubit gates [arxiv-2203.16302].

Three-dimensional transmons reduce TLS-related decoherence because their capacitor electric field is diluted into a much larger, cleaner 3D volume, so the qubit has lower participation of lossy amorphous surface/interface dielectrics where TLS reside. The review’s local summary states that TLS losses are tied to amorphous solids/interfaces in superconducting circuits and that geometry/material participation is central to TLS-induced relaxation/decoherence; 3D transmons are presented as an architecture that mitigates this by reducing electric-field overlap with those TLS-hosting regions [arxiv-1705.01108].

No exact numerical reduction factors or uncertainty-bearing values for this specific 3D-transmon claim are present in the retrieved local source summary [arxiv-1705.01108].

The claimed design advantage is that a **multi-path coupling scheme** can **strongly suppress residual static `ZZ` interaction between neighboring fluxonium qubits** while still allowing **large transverse `XX` coupling for fast gates**, enabling a compact scalable architecture [arxiv-2201.09374].

The local knowledge base says Nigg et al. reduce the effective Hilbert space by using the eigenstates of the associated **linearized circuit** as the basis, then treating the Josephson nonlinearity in that reduced low-energy space. This helps convergence because the circuits are **weakly anharmonic**, so the linear normal-mode basis is already close to the true eigenbasis and captures the relevant low-energy physics efficiently [arxiv-1204.0587].

Reducing the qubit–cable coupling improved the remote cross-resonance performance for the 1-m coaxial cable with narrow mode spacing. The source reports concurrences above 99.5% in selected regions after this change, with longer pulse durations near 386–400 ns and remaining cable-state constraints [arxiv-2404.10983].

The local knowledge base says the Purcell filter was implemented with open-circuited transmission-line stubs to modify the admittance seen by the qubit near its transition frequency, strongly inhibiting the output-environment Purcell decay channel while preserving coupling to a low-Q readout/reset cavity [arxiv-1003.0142].

However, the local source does not state why there were specifically two identical stubs placed above and below the chip axis.

The mechanism is **frequency-selective damping**: the bandpass Purcell filter makes the readout resonator strongly damped at its measurement/readout frequency while making the effective damping seen at the qubit frequency very small, because the filter’s admittance is off-resonant there. Thus measurement photons still leave the readout resonator quickly, but qubit-frequency vacuum noise is not efficiently coupled to the output line, suppressing Purcell decay without reducing measurement speed [arxiv-1504.06030].

The local KB source frames this as resolving the usual trade-off between **fast measurement** and **qubit relaxation through the readout resonator** by making the effective readout-resonator linewidth frequency dependent [arxiv-1504.06030].

In typical metal superconducting microwave circuits, the relevant circuit-QED modes are low-frequency collective electromagnetic modes, while bulk electronic plasma modes are far higher in energy and therefore effectively frozen out: Girvin’s notes state that superconductors have a gap frequency of order `100 GHz`, while metal plasma frequencies are of order `10^15 Hz`, far above microwave circuit frequencies. Thus bulk plasmon degrees of freedom are ignored because they are not part of the low-energy Hilbert space being quantized. [external-boulderschool.yale.edu-4267168c718e]

The review chose the transmon as its main superconducting artificial atom because, by the time of the review, circuit QED experiments had largely converged on the transmon qubit, which “dominates the field” due to its reduced charge-noise sensitivity while preserving sufficient anharmonicity for qubit operation [arxiv-2005.12667].

The local KB summary does not provide more exact numerical values, units, or uncertainties for this rationale [arxiv-2005.12667].

FAST DRAG suppresses the transmon `ef` leakage more effectively because it designs the in-phase envelope as a Fourier cosine series and analytically chooses coefficients to minimize spectral energy over selected unwanted frequency intervals, including the leakage transition. Conventional DRAG suppresses leakage less selectively; FAST DRAG explicitly shapes the pulse spectrum around the `ef` transition rather than relying only on the usual derivative quadrature correction [arxiv-2402.17757].

In the reported experiment, the transmon operated at `4.417 GHz` with anharmonicity `-212 MHz`. FAST DRAG-L achieved average gate error `(1.56 ± 0.07) × 10^-4` at `7.9 ns`, and FAST DRAG-L/HD DRAG-L kept leakage per gate at or below `3.0 × 10^-5` down to `6.25 ns`, reported as up to a `20-fold` leakage reduction versus Cosine DRAG-L at short durations [arxiv-2402.17757].

Both sources identify **in-situ tuning of the superconducting-qubit transition frequency** as the mechanism: changing the qubit frequency changes the wavelength/accumulated phase in the waveguide, thereby emulating or varying the effective separation/phase between coupling points or qubits [arxiv-1305.7135, nature-s41586-020-2529-9].

Kannan et al.’s **braided giant-atom** architecture adds the special capability that, at a **decoherence-free frequency**, relaxation into the waveguide is strongly suppressed while a **finite waveguide-mediated exchange interaction** remains between two qubits—so the qubits can be protected from spontaneous emission without turning off coherent coupling [nature-s41586-020-2529-9].

Fluxonium handled offset-charge variations by making the relevant wavefunctions nearly symmetric under offset-charge shifts, so all transition frequencies became insensitive to offset charge; experimentally, varying the gate charge over `0 ≤ n_g ≤ 1` produced no detectable frequency change within `6 MHz`, and a `12 h` run saw no observable jumps or drifts [arxiv-0906.0831].

That is stronger than the 2007 transmon mechanism: transmon charge noise protection comes from operating a Cooper-pair-box-derived circuit at large `E_J/E_C`, where charge dispersion of the low-lying levels is exponentially suppressed while anharmonicity falls only algebraically, leaving a controllable qubit [aps-10.1103-PhysRevA.76.042319; arxiv-cond-mat-0703002]. In short: fluxonium is described as offset-charge free for all transitions/states in the measured device, whereas the transmon design is charge-insensitive mainly because the low-lying qubit states have exponentially small residual charge dispersion [arxiv-0906.0831; arxiv-cond-mat-0703002].

The KB supports a survey, but only from summary-level evidence.

- **Fixed-frequency transmon, remote CR over coaxial cables:** uses one fixed-frequency qubit driven at the dressed frequency of another through multimode coaxial standing-wave modes, with echoed raised-cosine pulses. Simulations report average gate fidelity above 99.9% for 0.25 m and 0.5 m links with pulse durations about 150–170 ns; for 1 m links, concurrence above 99.5% is possible but requires weaker coupling and longer pulses near 386–400 ns. Main risks are multimode constraints, cable-state occupation, leakage, single-qubit fidelity degradation on long cables, and untested behavior with qubit decoherence/calibration errors [arxiv-2404.10983].

- **Capacitively coupled fluxonium CR:** demonstrates all-microwave selective-darkening CR: drive the control at the target frequency and add a direct drive to cancel target motion in the OFF-control state. A continuous off-resonant tone suppresses static ZZ from about 0.9 MHz to below 20 kHz. Reported 70 ns CXπ/CNOT-equivalent fidelity is 99.49(6)% by interleaved RB over 7 hours; fidelity stays above 99% across 50–100 ns, including a 54 ns gate at about 99.3%. Dominant failures are microwave pulse reflections requiring predistortion, subpar coherence/readout, about 94% initialization fidelity, and limited metrology below the observed infidelity [arxiv-2204.11829].

- **Inductively coupled fixed-frequency fluxonium CR/selective darkening:** treats two fluxoniums as a nearly transverse spin-1/2 pair, avoiding extra couplers and non-computational activation. It reports a 60 ns direct CXπ gate reaching 99.94% fidelity, remaining above 99.9% for 24 days without recalibration. Error analysis bounds extra coherent/non-decoherence error at about 2 × 10^-4 relative to a 60 ns identity, while simulations estimate coherent error near 10^-5, dominated by off-resonant control-qubit flips. Trade-offs are roughly three-hour tune-up, mixed initialized populations of 88% and 87%, and open classical-crosstalk risks in larger shared-junction layouts [arxiv-2407.15783].

- **Large fixed-frequency transmon allocation outside straddling:** KB describes a design-analysis route rather than a gate experiment: operate far-detuned CR outside the straddling regime to reduce frequency-collision constraints, accepting weaker CR interaction for better frequency-allocation flexibility. For 1024-qubit devices at a 0.1% two-qubit-gate infidelity threshold, reported 10% collision-free-yield tolerances are σf/2π = 6.8 MHz for square, 8.9 MHz for hexagonal, and 12.9 MHz for heavy-hexagonal layouts. Open risks are lack of experimental validation, assumptions of independent Gaussian frequency shifts, and missing variation in anharmonicity/coupling strength [arxiv-2605.07868].

Overall, the KB frames CR design as a control/scalability trade: transmon CR emphasizes frequency allocation and collision avoidance; remote transmon CR trades cable length and multimode leakage against nonlocal connectivity; fluxonium CR emphasizes high anharmonicity, sweet-spot operation, and selective-darkening cancellation, with current risks shifting toward pulse-line imperfections, tune-up overhead, initialization/readout, and multi-qubit crosstalk [arxiv-2404.10983][arxiv-2204.11829][arxiv-2407.15783][arxiv-2605.07868].

The KB treats Josephson junctions as both the nonlinear circuit element that defines qubit Hamiltonians and a fabrication-limited primitive whose spread, loss, and defects constrain scaling.

- **Circuit-design approaches:** Junctions appear as the nonlinear element in weakly anharmonic transmon/Xmon-style qubits, where the design couples a Josephson element to engineered capacitance and linear microwave environments; the Xmon is described as a planar, frequency-tunable grounded-transmon geometry with a cross-shaped coplanar-waveguide capacitor for scalable coupling and control [aps-10.1103-PhysRevLett.111.080502]. Fixed-frequency transmon processors are highlighted as vulnerable to frequency crowding, motivating post-fabrication junction tuning by laser annealing [arxiv-2009.00781].
- **Modeling and quantization:** The KB emphasizes three workflows: black-box quantization, which solves the linearized electromagnetic environment and then adds Josephson nonlinearity perturbatively [arxiv-1204.0587]; energy-participation-ratio quantization, which computes junction participation in electromagnetic modes and reports validation across 8 superconducting devices, 15 qubits, 8 cavity modes, and 1 waveguide system with about 1% frequency agreement and 5% agreement for large nonlinear couplings [arxiv-2010.00620]; and computer-aided lumped-circuit quantization from a user-specified circuit network [arxiv-2206.08320].
- **Fabrication and materials trade-offs:** The KB sources focus on Al/AlOx/Al junctions. A patch-integrated cross-type process is presented as a simplified route to reproducibly high-performance Xmon/transmon junctions [aip-10.1063-5.0037093]. Other sources frame junction reproducibility around junction-area fluctuation [arxiv-2210.15293], high-uniformity and stability fabrication on sapphire substrates [arxiv-2305.10956], and laser annealing as a yield-improvement method for scaled fixed-frequency processors [arxiv-2009.00781].
- **Dominant failure modes:** The KB identifies frequency crowding from junction-parameter spread as a scaling failure mode in fixed-frequency transmon architectures [arxiv-2009.00781], junction-area fluctuation as a reproducibility limiter [arxiv-2210.15293], and amorphous-material two-level systems as loss/noise defects that can couple strongly enough to qubits or resonators to be spectroscopically resolved and manipulated [arxiv-1705.01108].
- **Performance and validation:** Quantization validation is the most explicit numeric result in the retrieved KB: EPR calculations agree with measurements at about 1% for mode frequencies and 5% for large nonlinear couplings across the 8-device/15-qubit/8-cavity-mode/1-waveguide benchmark set [arxiv-2010.00620]. The Xmon source reports a coherent planar Josephson qubit suitable for scalable integrated circuits, but the retrieved KB evidence does not expose exact coherence numbers or uncertainties [aps-10.1103-PhysRevLett.111.080502].

- **Junction-first approaches:** PICT simplifies Al junction fabrication by avoiding bandage-style postprocessing and targets reproducibly high Xmon/transmon performance; reported median qubit relaxation was `T1 = 82 µs` across 18 measured qubits, with best `T1 = 128 µs` and median echo `T2 = 92 µs` [aip-10.1063-5.0037093]. Subtractive Al/AlOx/Al junction fabrication targets cleaner interfaces and process compatibility; the KB summary reports coherent qubits but does not expose wafer-scale statistics in the retrieved evidence [arxiv-2006.16862].

- **Junction variability sources:** Junction-area fluctuation is identified as a key source of frequency spread and reproducibility loss, linking lithographic area variation to Josephson critical-current variation and hence transmon frequency targeting errors [arxiv-2210.15293]. Separate Al/AlOx/Al work on sapphire focuses on high uniformity and stability, but the KB summary does not include integrated-qubit performance numbers [arxiv-2305.10956].

- **Surface/process approaches:** Surface-loss studies emphasize dielectric participation at metal–substrate, substrate–air, and metal–air interfaces as fabrication-linked coherence limits [arxiv-1509.03859; arxiv-1509.01854]. High-coherence transmon work targets substrate, metal, surface treatment, geometry, and packaging/process choices; the KB reports near-/millisecond-scale coherence studies but the retrieved summaries do not provide all exact process statistics [arxiv-2407.18778; nature-s41586-025-09687-4].

- **Wafer-/device-scale processing:** A 3D-integrated flip-chip architecture demonstrates CMOS-compatible superconducting-qubit processing on `200 mm` wafers, targeting scalable integration rather than only single-device coherence; the KB summary frames it as proof-of-concept wafer-scale processing [arxiv-2505.04337]. The Ta-on-Si millisecond 2D transmon result raises explicit open questions about reproducible transfer to wafer-scale fabrication and large processors [nature-s41586-025-09687-4].

- **Common failure modes/trade-offs:** Junction work primarily trades process simplicity, area control, and critical-current/frequency reproducibility against junction/interface cleanliness [aip-10.1063-5.0037093; arxiv-2210.15293; arxiv-2006.16862]. Surface/process work trades geometry, materials, substrate/interface preparation, and packaging against dielectric participation and other surface-linked losses [arxiv-1509.03859; arxiv-1509.01854; arxiv-2407.18778].

- **Scaling lesson:** The KB points to two coupled scaling requirements: control the junction enough to hit target frequencies reproducibly, and control surfaces/interfaces enough that high coherence survives process transfer. High single-device or small-batch coherence is not sufficient by itself; wafer-scale transmon fabrication needs quantified junction uniformity, surface-loss control, and demonstrated device distributions on production-relevant wafers [arxiv-2210.15293; arxiv-2505.04337; nature-s41586-025-09687-4].

Tunable-coupler approaches emphasize **idle decoupling plus fast flux-activated ZZ/CZ**, with experimental evidence. BBQ fixed-frequency transmons report off-state ZZ below 10 kHz, a 46 ns CZ with EPG 0.0015 ± 0.0001, and 19-hour no-recalibration stability, but short gates face non-adiabatic/leakage trade-offs and low-detuning pairs may need double-pulse iSWAP cancellation [arxiv-2101.07746]. Multi-chip floating couplers also experimentally reach zero-coupling points and a 56 ns inter-chip CZ at 99.13 ± 0.15%, averaging 98.61 ± 0.18% over seven hours without recalibration; scalability is modular, but only three device variants were tested [arxiv-2308.09240]. A SQUID parametric coupler cancels static ZZ to 0 ± 5.5 kHz and gives 70 ns p-SWAP CZ at 99.44 ± 0.09% and 30 ns SWAP-free CZ at 99.47 ± 0.07%, peaking 99.67 ± 0.14%, but high pump amplitudes cause rectification and multiphoton effects [arxiv-2305.02907]. A theoretical double-transmon coupler targets no residual coupling for highly detuned qubits, but the evidence is simulated/proposed rather than demonstrated [arxiv-2203.11451].

Tunable-gmon/fSim uses **direct adjustable exchange coupling** to realize continuous excitation-preserving gates. The local KB reports 525 benchmarked composite fSim gates, average Pauli errors of 1.2 × 10^-3 for iSWAP-like gates, 1.9 × 10^-3 for CPHASE gates, and 3.83 × 10^-3 per composite fSim, using about g_max/2π ≈ -45 MHz [arxiv-2001.08343]. Its strength is algorithmic flexibility and fast tunable coupling; its burdens are flux-pulse settling, leakage checks, extrapolated/higher-error regions near φ ≈ 0° or 360°, possible TLS-related error near φ ≈ 240°, and unclear scaling of composite calibrations to many simultaneous gates [arxiv-2001.08343].

Fluxonium multi-path / fluxonium-family approaches trade **large anharmonicity and weak idle hybridization** against architecture-specific calibration and scaling questions. Simulated multi-path fluxonium coupling combines inductive exchange with tiny capacitive coupling to cancel static ZZ, and studies CR CNOT plus differential AC-Stark CZ with low coherent errors, but this is mainly architectural/numerical and requires challenging ~100 pH inductive plus ~25 aF capacitive coupling [arxiv-2201.09374]. Experimentally, FTF fluxonium-transmon-fluxonium gates keep static ZZ at kHz levels across coupler flux, tune CZ operation over a 2 GHz range, reach 99.85–99.9% CZ fidelity, and 99.922 ± 0.009% with reinforcement learning; limits include flux-line heating, non-computational-state lifetimes, and short-gate coherent leakage [arxiv-2304.06087]. Low-frequency capacitively coupled fluxoniums demonstrated a 61.6 ns microwave CZ at 99.2 ± 0.1%, limited by higher-level decoherence and 3D-cavity addressability/crosstalk [arxiv-2011.02634]. Fixed-frequency inductively coupled fluxoniums demonstrated a 60 ns CXπ at 99.94%, above 99.9% for 24 days without recalibration, but tune-up took roughly three hours and larger devices must address classical crosstalk [arxiv-2407.15783].

LBI/RIP is the clearest **idle-first, microwave-activated ZZ** contrast. A six-qubit LBI processor uses multi-mode interference to cancel transverse exchange over a broad frequency range without flux bias; static ZZ is below 600 Hz across the device, including qubits only 10 MHz apart, while RIP gates energize bus modes to activate ZZ and reach fidelities up to 99.4%, with an interleaved-RB example EPG 0.0055 [arxiv-2406.11770]. Its advantages are low idle/spectator coupling and tolerance to frequency crowding; its disadvantages are slower/high-power off-resonant RIP activation, risk of multiphoton nonlinear processes, and incomplete spectator-error analysis for larger processors [arxiv-2406.11770].

Overall: **tunable couplers** give strong experimental speed/fidelity with active idle cancellation but add flux/pump controls and leakage/calibration modes; **gmon/fSim** gives flexible native gates but has flux-settling and composite-calibration overhead; **fluxonium multi-path/family gates** offer strong coherence, kHz-to-suppressed ZZ, and in some cases >99.9% demonstrated fidelity, but evidence ranges from simulation to small devices and scaling/crosstalk remain open; **LBI/RIP** best suppresses idle transverse/ZZ interactions in a six-qubit demonstration, but pays in RIP speed/power and unresolved spectator scaling.
